Series::sgn¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::sgn() const
Series& Series::sgn_() const

What It Does¶

Returns the sign of each element, generalized to complex numbers.

  • For a real input sgn() is -1, 0, or +1 — identical to sign().

  • For a complex input sgn() is the unit-modulus projection z / |z|, the point on the unit circle in the direction of z, and 0 at z = 0.

The complex case is why sgn() exists as a separate name: sign() has no ordering to fall back on for complex numbers and rejects them, while sgn() extends cleanly.

Magnitude Versus Direction¶

For every non-zero complex value, sgn() discards magnitude and preserves direction:

z = abs(z) * sgn(z)
abs(sgn(z)) = 1
angle(sgn(z)) = angle(z)

Multiplying z by any positive scale therefore leaves sgn(z) unchanged. This makes the method useful when only orientation matters, such as normalizing phasors or separating amplitude from phase before aggregation. Unlike dividing by abs() manually, sgn() defines the zero case explicitly and returns zero there instead of producing 0/0.

Parameters¶

None.

Returns¶

Series Same shape and dtype as the input. Real in, real out (-1 / 0 / +1); complex in, complex out on the unit circle (or 0).

Gradient¶

  • The real path is a step function — piecewise constant with a jump at 0. It carries no useful gradient, so an objective that reaches its input only through sgn() of a real series is disconnected and a reverse pass raises (the same contract as sign()).

  • The complex path, z / |z|, is a smooth composition of abs() and division away from the origin, so it is differentiable where z != 0.

In-Place Form¶

sgn_() is the in-place sibling of sgn(): it computes the same result and writes it back into self directly — mutating it (and any other handle sharing the same storage) instead of allocating a new Series — then returns a reference to self.

Despite being declared const at the call site — a quirk of how this method’s wrapper is generated, not a promise that self is left unchanged — sgn_() genuinely mutates the series it’s called on.

auto x = pluss::make_series({-3.0, 0.0, 4.0});

auto& ref = x.sgn_();
std::cout << "x=" << x << "\n";
std::cout << std::boolalpha << "same object: " << (&ref == &x);

Output¶

x=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-1, 0, 1]
same object: true

Examples¶

Example 1. On a real input sgn() matches sign().

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({-3.0, 0.0, 2.5}).sgn()
) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-1.0000, 0.0000, 1.0000]

Example 2. On a complex input sgn() is z / |z|, with 0 mapped to 0.

auto z = pluss::make_series(
    {std::complex<float>{3, 4}, {-1, 0}, {0, 2}, {0, 0}});

pluss::series::print(std::cout, z.sgn()) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=complex64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[(0.6000+0.8000j), (-1.0000+0.0000j), (0.0000+1.0000j), (0.0000+0.0000j)]

(3 + 4j) / 5 = 0.6 + 0.8j; (0 + 2j) / 2 = 1j; 0 stays 0.

Example 3. Every non-zero result has modulus 1. Here z is assembled from its parts with pluss::series::complex.

auto z = pluss::series::complex(
    pluss::make_series({3.0f, -1.0f, 0.0f, 0.0f}),
    pluss::make_series({4.0f,  0.0f, 2.0f, 0.0f}));

pluss::series::print(std::cout, z.sgn().abs()) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float32, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[1.0000, 1.0000, 1.0000, 0.0000]

Example 4. sign() rejects complex input; sgn() is the generalization to reach for.

auto z = pluss::make_series(
    {std::complex<float>{3, 4}, {-1, 0}, {0, 2}, {0, 0}});

try {
  std::cout << z.sign();
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

sign: not supported for complex dtypes; use sgn()

Example 5. The complex path remains differentiable away from zero. Here the objective keeps only the real coordinate of the unit direction. At 3 + 4j, the resulting source sensitivity is 0.128 - 0.096j.

auto z = pluss::series::complex(pluss::make_series({3.0f}),
                                pluss::make_series({4.0f}));
z.tracks_slope_(true);
z.sgn().real().sum().reverse();
pluss::series::print(std::cout, z.sensitivity()) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[1], strides=[1], dtype=complex64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[(0.1280-0.0960j)]

The derivative depends on direction because normalization couples the real and imaginary coordinates. It is not the identity gradient.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • On a real input sgn() and sign() are the same function; the difference only shows up for complex dtypes.

  • sgn(0) is 0 in both the real and complex cases — it is not projected to a point on the unit circle.

  • sgn() preserves shape and dtype. It normalizes each element independently; it does not normalize a vector or matrix as a whole.

  • The real path is non-differentiable (a reverse pass through it alone raises); the complex path is differentiable away from the origin.

Summary¶

sgn() is the sign, generalized to the complex plane:

  • real: -1 / 0 / +1, exactly like sign()

  • complex: z / |z| (unit modulus), 0 at the origin

  • real path non-differentiable; complex path differentiable where z != 0

See Also¶

  • Series::sign: the real-only sign; raises on complex input.

  • Series::abs: the magnitude that sgn() divides out.

  • Series::angle: the phase — sgn(z) is polar(1, angle(z)).

  • pluss::series::complex / pluss::series::polar: build a complex series.
